claims.evidence: This is a finding from the insect analysis.

claims.claim: Several studies explored the link between Nee and genome size in insects by focussing on social complexity as a proxy, but with contrasting outcomes.
claims.source: As eusociality appears to bring about selection relaxation (Imrit et al., 2020; Kapheim et al., 2015; Weyna and Romiguier, 2021), several studies explored the link between Nee and genome size in this taxon by focussing on social complexity as a proxy, but with contrasting outcomes: Mikhailova et al., 2024 find bigger genome size associated with eusociality in Hymenoptera, but the opposite trend in Blattodea; in contrast and partially in accordance with our findings, Kapheim et al., 2015 and Koshikawa et al., 2008 report less abundant TEs in eusocial hymenopters and smaller genomes in eusocial termites, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous research with citations.

claims.claim: Genome size seems to be subject to different evolutionary pressures within different insect orders.
claims.source: First, and specifically relative to insects, genome size seems to be subject to different evolutionary pressures – either selective or neutral – within different insect orders (Cong et al., 2022), implying that increased drift might not necessarily produce the same effect on genome size across all insect groups.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Increased drift might not necessarily produce the same effect on genome size across all insect groups.
claims.source: First, and specifically relative to insects, genome size seems to be subject to different evolutionary pressures – either selective or neutral – within different insect orders (Cong et al., 2022), implying that increased drift might not necessarily produce the same effect on genome size across all insect groups.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation of different patterns in different insect orders.

claims.claim: The five defined clades cover quite different time scales.
claims.source: More generally, the five defined clades cover quite different time scales: insects and molluscs have much more ancient origins than mammals and birds, and such distant groups also evolve at very different evolutionary rates, making it difficult to characterize the evolution of their traits on the same evolutionary scale.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the phylogenetic scale of the study.

claims.claim: The results are valuable in highlighting the absence of relationship between genetic drift and genome size variation in the long-term evolution of broad groups.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the results are still valuable in highlighting the absence of relationship between genetic drift and genome size variation in the long-term evolution of such broad groups, in contrast to previous work focusing at the population level or on recently diverged species (Cui et al., 2019; Mérel et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the contribution of the study.

claims.claim: Comparing very distantly related species might overshadow any relationship between genome size and Nee.
claims.source: At the same time, as noted by Mérel et al., 2025, comparing very distantly related species – as the insect and molluscan species of our dataset – might overshadow any relationship between genome size and Nee, either due to dN/dS predicting power being weakened by branch saturation, deep Nee fluctuations not being detected by our methods, or to additional factors affecting long-term genome size evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a potential limitation discussed with reference to previous work.

claims.claim: The findings do not support the quantity of non-coding DNA being driven in a nearly-neutral fashion by genetic drift.
claims.source: Our findings do not support the quantity of non-coding DNA being driven in a nearly-neutral fashion by genetic drift.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: The results not only reject the theory of extra non-coding DNA being costly for its point mutational risk, but also challenge the more general idea of its accumulation depending on other kinds of detrimental effects.
claims.source: Notably, these results not only reject the theory of extra non-coding DNA being costly for its point mutational risk, but also challenges the more general idea of its accumulation depending on other kinds of detrimental effects, such as increased replication, pervasive transcription, or ectopic recombination.
claims.evidence: This is a broader interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: The results can be considered more general than a mere rejection of the MHH hypothesis, as they do not support any theory predicting that species with low Nee would accumulate more non-coding DNA.
claims.source: Therefore, our results can be considered more general than a mere rejection of the MHH hypothesis, as they do not support any theory predicting that species with low Nee would accumulate more non-coding DNA.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claims.claim: The proliferation of TEs can, under comparable drift levels, give place to lineage-specific outcomes that mostly do not seem to depend on effective population size.
claims.source: In agreement with previous analyses (Pasquesi et al., 2018), we find that the proliferation of TEs in particular can, under comparable drift levels, give place to lineage-specific outcomes that mostly do not seem to depend on effective population size.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion consistent with previous research.

claims.claim: The results contrast with those of other large-scale analyses which support the predictions of the drift-barrier hypothesis for a general impact of Nee on other genomic features.
claims.source: These results contrast with those of other large-scale analyses which instead support the predictions of the drift-barrier hypothesis for a general impact of Nee on other genomic features, notably mutation rate (Bergeron et al., 2023; Lynch et al., 2023; Wang and Obbard, 2023) and splicing accuracy (Bénitière et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with other research findings.

claims.claim: In the framework of the MHH, the success of nearly-neutral alleles depends on the combination of both Nee and liability to mutation of non-coding DNA.
claims.source: To put this in perspective, it should be emphasized that, in the framework of the MHH, the success of nearly-neutral alleles depends on the combination of both Nee and liability to mutation of non-coding DNA (Lynch et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the theoretical framework with citation.

claims.claim: The study assumed the same distribution of selective effect and a constant activity of TEs in all species and among TE insertions.
claims.source: In the case of TEs, inherently assuming the same distribution of selective effect and a constant activity in all species and among TE insertions was assumed.
claims.evidence: This describes an assumption of the study.

claims.claim: TEs are subject to waves of activity rather than a uniform pace of transposition.
claims.source: However, it is known that TEs are subject to waves of activity rather than a uniform pace of transposition (Arkhipova, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge as cited.

claims.claim: Different levels of hazard are likely acting across genomes due to different 'host-parasite' dynamics in different animal groups.
claims.source: Moreover, given the broad phylogenetic scale of our dataset, it is likely for different levels of hazard to be acting across genomes due to different "host-parasite" dynamics in different animal groups (Ågren and Wright, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about potential variation across lineages, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: TE silencing mechanisms evolve differently across lineages and might influence the degree of genome expansion.
claims.source: Such coevolutionary dynamics are, for example, determined by TE silencing mechanisms, which evolve differently across lineages and might influence the degree of genome expansion (Lechner et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Treating TEs as universally slightly deleterious alleles might be an oversimplified model.
claims.source: In general, because of their complex interactions with genomes, TEs are especially likely to deviate from the assumption of gradually mutating sequences. Therefore, treating them as universally slightly deleterious alleles might be an oversimplified model.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the limitations of the MHH framework for TEs.

claims.claim: The big genomes of salamanders are not related to small Nee.
claims.source: For instance, while the big genomes of salamanders are not related to small Nee, the low synonymous substitution rates and low degree of deletions due to ectopic recombination suggest weak mutational hazard of TEs that possibly contributes to the maintenance of genomic gigantism in this group (Frahry et al., 2015; Mohlhenrich and Mueller, 2016; Rios-Carlos et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is an example from previous research as cited.

claims.claim: Lineage-specific TE dynamics might underlie different genomic architectures.
claims.source: Additionally, lineage-specific TE dynamics themselves might underlie different genomic architectures: for example, mammalian genomes are generally characterized by one preponderant type of active element and by a long-term retention of old TEs (Osmanski et al., 2023; Sotero-Caio et al., 2017), as in human where a very small proportion of active elements (<0.05%) is unlikely to impose a mutation rate causing genome size variation (Mills et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Squamate and teleost fish genomes are smaller and characterized by several, simultaneously active and less abundant TE types.
claims.source: Conversely, squamate and teleost fish genomes are smaller and characterized by several, simultaneously active and less abundant TE types (Duvernell et al., 2004; Furano et al., 2004; Novick et al., 2009; Pasquesi et al., 2018; Volff et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Different patterns of genomic organization seem associated with different rates of elements' turnover.
claims.source: These different patterns of genomic organization seem overall associated with different rates of elements' turnover (Bennett and Riley, 1997; Lavoie et al., 2013; Novick et al., 2009; Volff et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Large-scale deletions can be as important as DNA gain in determining genome size.
claims.source: Finally, Kapusta et al., 2017 showed that large-scale deletions can be as important as DNA gain in determining genome size, thus questioning the assumption of the rate of elements insertion being greater than their removal rate (Lynch, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Deletion bias could drive the divergence of genome size across lineages.
claims.source: This implies that the contribution of TEs constitutes just one side of the coin and that deletion bias could also drive the divergence of genome size across lineages, as suggested by several studies linking negatively deletion rates with genome size (Frahry et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2022; Kapusta et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: In Anolis lizards, the ability of TEs to reach fixation can vary between populations of the same species according to population size.
claims.source: In Anolis lizards, the ability of TEs to reach fixation can vary between populations of the same species according to population size (Ruggiero et al., 2017; Tollis and Boissinot, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Nee was found to negatively correlate with genome size and TE expansion at the intraspecific level in Drosophila suzukii.
claims.source: Furthermore, Nee was found to negatively correlate with genome size and TE expansion at the intraspecific level in Drosophila suzukii (Mérel et al., 2021) and at the interspecific level in fruit flies (Mérel et al., 2025), asellid isopods (Lefébure et al., 2017), and killifishes (Cui et al., 2019), supporting the role of genetic drift in determining recent differences in genome size among closely related animal species.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: An increase in genetic drift seems to lead to the short-term accumulation of transposable elements, but this process is not visible in the long term.
claims.source: In a nutshell, although an increase in genetic drift seems to lead to the short-term accumulation of transposable elements, this process is not visible in the long term, suggesting that it fades over time.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion reconciling short-term and long-term findings.

claims.claim: A general mechanism of selection preventing the proliferation of non-coding DNA and TEs in animals might exist but its results be detectable only at a sufficiently short evolutionary time.
claims.source: A general mechanism of selection preventing the proliferation of non-coding DNA and TEs in animals might exist but its results be detectable only at a sufficiently short evolutionary time.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the temporal scale of selection effects.

results.result: Assembly size strongly correlates with C-value (r=0.97, p<0.001) but tends to underestimate genome size, particularly for larger genomes. This underestimation is independent of sequencing technology (long vs. short reads). The authors conclude that their selected assemblies provide reliable genome size measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 provide strong statistical evidence for the correlation and systematic bias. The high correlation coefficient and the lack of technology-dependent effects (C24) support the reliability assessment (C74-C75). The quality filtering criteria (contig N50 ≥50 kb, BUSCO ≥70%) provide additional confidence in the dataset quality.

results.result: TEs are major drivers of genome size variation across animals, showing very strong positive correlations both across the whole dataset and within taxa (Table 1, Figure 4A). Birds represent a notable exception with weaker correlations. Genome duplications contribute minimally compared to TEs.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C30 provide comprehensive statistical evidence across multiple clades. The strong correlations (adjusted-R²=0.417 overall, higher within most clades per Table 1), consistency with prior literature (C77-C78), and comparative analysis showing minimal contribution from duplications (C27-C29) strongly support this major finding. The avian exception (C26) is appropriately noted.

results.result: dN/dS serves as a reliable proxy for long-term effective population size (Nee). Bio++ and Coevol dN/dS estimates are highly concordant with each other (r=0.902-0.887, p<0.001) and scale positively with life-history traits (body mass, longevity) as expected under population genetics theory.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 provide strong statistical validation through PIC analysis and comparison of two independent methods. The concordance between methods (C38, C92) and expected relationships with LHTs (C35, C39) support the reliability of dN/dS as a Nee proxy. The improved correlations after removing short/long branches (C36-C37) demonstrate methodological rigor. The theoretical foundation (C31-C34) is well-established.

results.result: No evidence was found for a relationship between dN/dS (as a proxy for Nee) and genome size or TE content across all animal species analyzed. This contradicts the predictions of the Mutational Hazard Hypothesis at broad phylogenetic scales.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 report null results from PIC analyses that are statistically rigorous and phylogenetically controlled. The consistency across different analytical approaches (full and trimmed phylogenies) strengthens confidence. This is the primary negative finding (C8, C72, C120) that challenges the MHH. The lack of association is appropriately interpreted as absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence, but the large sample size (807 species) provides adequate power.

results.result: Clade-specific analyses reveal heterogeneous patterns: negative correlations between dN/dS and TE content in mammals, positive correlations in ray-finned fishes, and inconsistent patterns in birds and insects. These lineage-specific patterns show no consistent response to Nee variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C53 report statistically significant but weak correlations (adjusted-R² values 0.004-0.063) with inconsistent directions across clades. While the statistical tests are appropriate, the very low explained variance raises questions about biological significance. The opposite patterns in different clades (C44-C46) are intriguing but the weak effect sizes and multiple comparisons without correction for multiple testing create uncertainty about the robustness of these clade-specific findings.

results.result: Recent TE content (divergence <5% from consensus) shows weak positive correlation with dN/dS across all species (adjusted-R²=0.012, p=0.003), but clade-specific patterns are inconsistent: negative associations in fishes, positive in mammals, with different methods (PIC vs. Coevol) sometimes yielding opposite results.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C71 report weak correlations with inconsistent patterns across clades and methods. The very low explained variance (1.2% overall) and contradictory results between PIC and Coevol approaches (C61-C64) undermine confidence. The 5% divergence threshold for defining 'recent' TEs is applied uniformly across species with different mutation rates and generation times (acknowledged in text), which may introduce noise. The biological interpretation of these weak, inconsistent patterns is unclear.

results.result: Life-history traits show clade-specific associations with TE content and genome size: in mammals, TE content correlates opposite to MHH predictions (negatively with traits indicating low Nee); in fishes, patterns are consistent with MHH; in birds, genome size and TE content show decoupled patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 and C102-C106 are supported by Coevol analyses (Table 2) showing consistent patterns within clades. The mammalian pattern (C55, C102-C104) is particularly robust and corroborates prior work (Roddy et al., 2021). The fish pattern (C54, C105) is consistent with previous findings (Yi and Streelman, 2005). The avian decoupling (C56-C57, C60, C106) is biologically plausible given the narrow genome size range in birds. These clade-specific patterns are more convincing than the weak dN/dS correlations.

results.result: Genomic duplications have negligible effect on the relationship between dN/dS and genome size. Removing 24 species with >30% duplicated BUSCO genes produced similar results, and the contribution of duplicated genes to genome size is minimal compared to TEs.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 report a sensitivity analysis showing consistent results after removing high-duplication species. Claims C84-C85 provide comparative evidence that TEs explain far more variance than duplications. This effectively rules out genome duplication as a confounding factor. The analysis is appropriate and the conclusion is well-supported.

results.result: The dnaPipeTE method provides reliable TE quantification for large-scale analysis despite known limitations (underestimation of satellites, inability to detect ancient TEs). Validation against EarlGrey shows strong concordance (r=0.88-0.90, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 acknowledge methodological limitations while providing empirical validation. The comparison with EarlGrey on 29 dipteran genomes (Figure 3) shows strong agreement. The authors appropriately note that satellite underestimation may affect some species (particularly birds) but argue the effect is minimal on general trends. The read-based approach (C76) avoids assembly completeness issues. The validation is adequate for the study's purposes.

results.result: The dN/dS calculation methodology included rigorous filtering by branch length and topology, with analyses robust to species pruning. The approach captures long-term Nee rather than short-term fluctuations, as supported by theoretical considerations and prior validation studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 describe methodological rigor with appropriate filtering and sensitivity analyses. Claims C90-C91 provide theoretical justification for using dN/dS as a long-term Nee proxy, supported by citations to population genetics theory and prior validation work (Latrille et al., 2021). The distinction between long-term (dN/dS) and short-term (polymorphism-based) Nee estimates is important for interpreting the results.

results.result: Phylogenetic structure strongly influences the data: major clades occupy distinct genome size ranges regardless of dN/dS variation. Not accounting for phylogenetic non-independence leads to artifactual positive correlations between genome size and Nee proxies.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C99 highlight a critical methodological point. The observation that mammals have large genomes and low Nee while insects have small genomes and high Nee (C95-C96) creates phylogenetic confounding. The demonstration that uncorrected analyses yield artifactual results (C94, Figure 4B-C) while PIC analyses do not (C97-C99) is convincing. This explains why early MHH studies without phylogenetic correction found support. The point is well-made and important.

results.result: TE dynamics vary according to lineage-specific patterns, and genetic drift is not the predominant force driving long-term genome size evolution in animals. The results reject not only the MHH but any theory predicting that low Nee species accumulate more non-coding DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C73 state the main conclusions, which are supported by the comprehensive analyses showing no consistent relationship between Nee proxies and genome size/TE content across animals (C40-C47) and heterogeneous clade-specific patterns (C42-C53). Claim C122-C123 appropriately broaden the interpretation beyond just the MHH. The conclusion is well-supported by the data, though the weak clade-specific patterns introduce some uncertainty about the strength of lineage-specific effects.

results.result: The five clades analyzed cover very different evolutionary timescales, which may limit detection of Nee-genome size relationships. The results are valuable for highlighting absence of relationships at broad phylogenetic scales but comparing distantly related species might overshadow relationships detectable at finer scales.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 acknowledge important limitations of the phylogenetic scale. The observation that insects and molluscs are much more ancient than mammals and birds (C117) is factually correct. The interpretation that this limits comparability (C119) is reasonable and supported by citation to Mérel et al., 2025. The authors appropriately frame their results as applying to long-term evolution (C118) while acknowledging that finer-scale patterns might differ. This is a fair assessment of scope and limitations.

results.result: The MHH framework assumes constant TE activity and uniform selective effects across species, but TEs actually show waves of activity, lineage-specific host-parasite dynamics, and variable silencing mechanisms. Treating TEs as universally slightly deleterious may be oversimplified.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C130 provide important theoretical context for interpreting the negative results. The assumptions of the MHH (C125-C126) are clearly stated. The evidence that TEs deviate from these assumptions (C127-C129, supported by multiple citations) is well-documented. The conclusion that the MHH model may be oversimplified for TEs (C130) is a reasonable inference. This discussion strengthens the interpretation of why the MHH predictions are not supported.

results.result: Evidence from population-level and closely related species studies shows that increased genetic drift can lead to short-term TE accumulation, but this process is not visible in long-term evolution. A general selection mechanism against TE proliferation might exist but be detectable only at short evolutionary timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138 cite multiple studies showing Nee effects at fine phylogenetic scales. The synthesis (C139-C140) reconciling short-term and long-term patterns is a reasonable interpretation that explains the apparent contradiction between this study and prior work. This is speculative (C140) but well-grounded in the comparative evidence. The temporal scale hypothesis is testable and provides a coherent framework for understanding the field.

results.result: The study demonstrates that transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genome size variation across 807 animal species (vertebrates, molluscs, and insects), with a very strong positive correlation between TE content and genome size found both across the whole dataset and within taxa.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. The editor states the study 'provides the convincing negative result that effective population size scales neither with the content of transposable elements nor with overall genome size,' implicitly accepting the TE-genome size correlation. Reviewer 1 notes 'the strength of this analysis is that it is comprehensive and treats all the genomes with the same pipeline, making comparisons more convincing.' Reviewer 2 states 'The general conclusions of this paper are supported by a powerful dataset of phylogenetically diverse species.'

results.result: The study validates that life-history traits (LHTs) and dN/dS ratios are reliable proxies for effective population size (Nee), with Bio++ dN/dS scaling positively with body mass and longevity, and Coevol dN/dS values being highly concordant with Bio++ dN/dS.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the methodological validation without challenge. Reviewer 2 notes 'the use of dN/dS and life history traits as reliable proxies for effective population size' as part of the study's approach, treating it as valid. The editor's summary accepts that the study uses 'the ratio of synonymous to nonsynonymous mutations in coding sequence as a measure of overall strength of purifying selection, which serves as a proxy for effective population size over time' without questioning this approach.

results.result: The study finds no evidence for increased genetic drift (low Nee) resulting in accumulation of TEs across animals, with no statistical support for a relationship between dN/dS and TE content/genome size across all species, contradicting the Mutational Hazard Hypothesis (MHH).
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this negative result as the study's main finding. The editor states the study 'provides the convincing negative result that effective population size scales neither with the content of transposable elements nor with overall genome size.' Reviewer 1 emphasizes 'The data convincingly demonstrates that it is unlikely that effective population size has a strong effect on TE content and, by extension, overall genome size.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The results suggest that overall, lineages with lower effective population sizes do not exhibit increases in repeat content or genome size. This contrasts with expectations from the MHH.'

results.result: Within more closely related clades, only isolated and weak associations emerge, with clade-specific patterns showing negative correlations in mammals (opposite to MHH predictions), positive correlations in fishes (consistent with MHH), and complex patterns in birds and insects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these clade-specific findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes the exception 'except for birds, which are weird,' acknowledging the heterogeneous patterns. The editor's statement that 'there is still no simple, global hypothesis that can explain the observed variation in transposable element content and genome size in animals' implicitly accepts the lineage-specific patterns as valid findings.

results.result: TE dynamics vary according to lineage-specific patterns, with the proliferation of TEs giving rise to lineage-specific outcomes that mostly do not depend on effective population size, highlighting heterogeneous patterns within clades with no consistent response of genome size and TE dynamics to Nee variations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation as the study's conclusion. The editor states 'These observations demonstrate that there is still no simple, global hypothesis that can explain the observed variation in transposable element content and genome size in animals.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The authors speculate that changes in genome size may be driven by lineage-specific host-TE conflicts rather than effective population size' without challenging this interpretation.

results.result: Assembly size is strongly positively correlated with C-value (r=0.97, p<0.001) and can overall approximate genome size quite well, though assembly sizes tend to underestimate genome size as it increases, with no effect from sequencing read type after quality filtering.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly supports this methodological validation, stating 'The use of C-values rather than assembly size for many species (when available) helps to mitigate the challenges associated with underrepresentation of repetitive regions in short-read based genome assemblies.' The reviewer notes this as a strength and raises no concerns about the assembly size approximation.

results.result: The avian clade deviates from the general pattern, with a weaker correlation between TE content and genome size compared to other clades, and previous studies finding relatively weak correlations between TE content and genome size in birds.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledges this finding, noting the data 'convincingly demonstrates' the general pattern 'except for birds, which are weird.' This comment accepts the avian deviation as a valid observation without challenging the finding.

results.result: While dnaPipeTE is known to underestimate satellite content, the strong correlation between repeat content and genome size and consistency with earlGrey results indicate that the dnaPipeTE method is pertinent for large-scale analysis.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 initially raised concerns about 'possible biases in the author's data due to their approach to TE annotation' but states in the final review that 'The authors have sufficiently acknowledged and addressed these concerns in their revised manuscript. I note no further weaknesses.' This indicates acceptance of the methodological approach after revision.

results.result: Not treating species traits as phylogenetically non-independent leads to artifactual results; with phylogenetic correction, the main clades are each confined to separate genome size ranges regardless of their dN/dS variation, and relying on non-phylogenetically corrected models can result in spurious positive scaling.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 emphasizes this as a strength: 'tested for correlations between these proxies and repeat content while accounting for phylogenetic nonindependence' and notes 'both the phylogenetic breadth of species considered and the approaches employed make the results highly convincing.' The importance of phylogenetic correction is implicitly accepted by all reviewers.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on genome size validation (C22-C24, C74-C75). Both evaluations support the methodological approach with complete claim overlap. OpenEval emphasizes statistical evidence and quality filtering, while peer review highlights the use of C-values to mitigate assembly biases.

Strong agreement on the main negative finding (C8, C40-C41, C47, C72, C120). Both evaluations support the null result that effective population size does not correlate with TE content/genome size. OpenEval notes adequate statistical power with 807 species; peer reviewers describe this as 'convincing' and the study's primary contribution.

Both support the TE-genome size correlation (C25-C30, C6, C77-C79). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation with adjusted-R² values and notes the avian exception. Peer reviewers accept this as foundational, emphasizing the comprehensive pipeline and phylogenetic diversity as strengths.

Both support dN/dS validation as Nee proxy (C35-C39, C92-C93). OpenEval emphasizes concordance between methods and PIC analysis rigor. Peer reviewers accept this methodological approach without challenge, treating dN/dS and life history traits as reliable proxies.

Both support the main conclusion about lineage-specific effects (C10, C73, C123). OpenEval notes the conclusion is well-supported despite weak clade-specific patterns. Peer reviewers accept that no simple global hypothesis explains variation, emphasizing lineage-specific host-TE conflicts.

Divergent evaluations of clade-specific patterns (C42-C53, C9). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to weak effect sizes (adjusted-R² 0.004-0.063) and lack of multiple testing correction. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting heterogeneous patterns without challenging statistical robustness. Peer review also includes Coevol results (C58, C102-C106) not in OpenEval R5.

Both support the importance of phylogenetic correction (C94, C97, C99). OpenEval emphasizes how uncorrected analyses yield artifactual results while PIC analyses avoid confounding. Peer reviewers highlight phylogenetic nonindependence accounting as a key strength making results 'highly convincing.'

Both support TE annotation methodology (C82-C83). OpenEval notes adequate validation with EarlGrey comparison and appropriate acknowledgment of limitations. Peer reviewer initially raised concerns but accepted the approach after revision, stating concerns were 'sufficiently acknowledged and addressed.'

Partial overlap on clade-specific Coevol patterns (C102-C106, C58). OpenEval supports these findings as more convincing than weak dN/dS correlations, noting mammalian and fish patterns corroborate prior work. Peer review R4 accepts clade-specific findings broadly without detailed evaluation of Coevol vs PIC methods.

Minimal overlap on avian exception (C26). OpenEval notes the avian exception to TE-genome size correlation as appropriately documented. Peer reviewer acknowledges birds as 'weird' exception, accepting the deviation without challenge.

OpenEval evaluates TE age correlations (C61-C71) as UNCERTAIN due to weak effect sizes (1.2% variance), contradictory results between methods, and uniform 5% divergence threshold issues. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports the sensitivity analysis ruling out genome duplication as confounding factor (C48-C49, C84-C85), showing TEs explain far more variance. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports methodological rigor and theoretical justification for dN/dS as long-term Nee proxy (C88-C91), distinguishing from short-term polymorphism-based estimates. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports acknowledgment of phylogenetic scale limitations (C117-C119), noting insects/molluscs are more ancient than mammals/birds, limiting comparability. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports theoretical context explaining why MHH assumptions may not apply to TEs (C125-C130), noting TEs deviate from neutral mutation assumptions. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports temporal scale hypothesis reconciling short-term vs long-term Nee patterns (C137-C140), providing framework for understanding contradictions with prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
